questions.stem: A Lambda function's dependencies, including machine learning libraries, are larger than the .zip deployment package size limit. How should the developer package the function?

options.text: As several .zip files uploaded together
options.rationale: A function has one deployment package.

options.text: As a container image stored in Amazon ECR
options.rationale: Container images allow much larger function packages than .zip archives.

options.text: With the libraries listed in environment variables
options.rationale: Environment variables cannot hold libraries.

options.text: With a longer function timeout
options.rationale: Timeout does not change the package size limit.

questions.explanation: Use container images for large dependencies; use .zip and layers for smaller packages.

questions.stem: An Amazon ECS service uses rolling deployments. When a new revision's tasks keep failing health checks, the team wants the deployment to stop and return to the last working revision automatically. What should the developer enable?

options.text: A Fargate Spot capacity provider for the service's tasks
options.rationale: Spot capacity changes pricing, not deployment behavior.

options.text: A larger task memory size
options.rationale: More memory does not detect failed deployments.

options.text: The deployment circuit breaker with rollback
options.rationale: The circuit breaker detects a failing deployment and rolls back to the last completed one.

options.text: ECR tag immutability
options.rationale: Immutable tags protect images, not running deployments.

questions.explanation: ECS rolling deployments can roll back automatically with the deployment circuit breaker.

questions.stem: A team wants to run containers on Amazon ECS without provisioning, patching or scaling any EC2 instances. Which launch type should the developer specify in the service?

options.text: The EC2 launch type
options.rationale: The EC2 launch type runs tasks on instances the team manages.

options.text: An Auto Scaling group of Spot Instances
options.rationale: The team would still manage those instances.

options.text: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
options.rationale: Beanstalk is an application platform, not an ECS launch type.

options.text: AWS Fargate
options.rationale: Fargate runs tasks on serverless compute that AWS manages.

questions.explanation: Fargate removes server management for ECS and EKS workloads.

questions.stem: A team deploys a Lambda function with AWS SAM. New versions should receive 10 percent of traffic first, then all traffic a few minutes later, and roll back automatically if a CloudWatch alarm fires. What should the developer configure?

options.text: A canary deployment preference with the alarm listed
options.rationale: SAM's DeploymentPreference creates a CodeDeploy canary deployment that shifts traffic in two steps and watches alarms.

options.text: An all-at-once deployment preference with the alarm listed
options.rationale: All traffic moves at once, so there is no small first step.

options.text: Two Lambda layers, one for each version
options.rationale: Layers share code; they do not shift traffic.

options.text: Reserved concurrency of 10 percent on the new version
options.rationale: Concurrency limits do not route traffic between versions.

questions.explanation: Canary moves traffic in two increments, linear in equal steps, and all-at-once immediately.

questions.stem: A team wants to release a new version of an application alongside the current one, then move traffic over and be able to switch back immediately if problems appear. Which deployment strategy fits?

options.text: In-place rolling
options.rationale: Instances are updated in batches, so going back means redeploying.

options.text: Blue/green
options.rationale: The old environment stays in place, so traffic can be switched back quickly.

options.text: All at once
options.rationale: Every target is updated together with no previous environment to return to.

options.text: Recreate
options.rationale: The old version is removed before the new one starts.

questions.explanation: Blue/green keeps two environments, which makes rollback a traffic switch.

questions.stem: A team uses AWS CodePipeline. Each push to the main branch should start the pipeline, and a team lead must sign off before the production stage runs. Which steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a manual approval action before the production stage
options.rationale: The pipeline pauses until someone approves or rejects.

options.text: Add CloudFormation drift detection to the build stage
options.rationale: Drift detection compares stacks to templates; it is not an approval.

options.text: Use a source action connected to the repository that starts the pipeline on each push
options.rationale: A connection-based source action detects pushes and starts the pipeline.

options.text: Schedule the pipeline to run every night with Amazon EventBridge Scheduler
options.rationale: A nightly run does not start the pipeline on each push.

options.text: Give the team lead permission to edit the buildspec file
options.rationale: Editing the build does not create an approval gate.

questions.explanation: CodePipeline orchestrates stages; approvals add a human gate between them.

questions.stem: A CloudFormation stack update must roll back automatically if an application error alarm goes into ALARM state during the update or shortly after. What should the developer configure?

options.text: Termination protection on the stack
options.rationale: Termination protection prevents stack deletion.

options.text: A DeletionPolicy of Retain on each resource
options.rationale: Retain keeps resources when they are deleted; it does not watch alarms.

options.text: Rollback triggers on the stack that monitor the alarm
options.rationale: CloudFormation watches the alarms during the update and a monitoring period, and rolls back if one fires.

options.text: Drift detection that runs automatically after each update
options.rationale: Drift detection reports manual changes; it does not roll back.

questions.explanation: Rollback triggers connect CloudWatch alarms to CloudFormation updates.

questions.stem: Before updating a production CloudFormation stack, a developer wants to see which resources will be added, changed or replaced. What should the developer create?

options.text: A stack set
options.rationale: Stack sets deploy stacks across accounts and Regions.

options.text: A drift detection report
options.rationale: Drift shows differences from the current template, not from a proposed update.

options.text: A nested stack
options.rationale: Nested stacks organize templates; they do not preview updates.

options.text: A change set
options.rationale: A change set previews the changes an update will make before you run it.

questions.explanation: Change sets show the effect of an update, including replacements, before it happens.

questions.stem: A network stack creates a VPC. A separate application stack must use that VPC's ID without hardcoding it. How should the developer share the value?

options.text: Export it as an output of the network stack and use Fn::ImportValue
options.rationale: Exports share values between stacks in the same account and Region.

options.text: Copy the ID into the application template by hand
options.rationale: Hardcoded IDs break when the network stack changes.

options.text: Reference the network stack's VPC from the application stack with Fn::GetAtt
options.rationale: GetAtt reads attributes of resources in the same template.

options.text: Pass the ID through a Lambda environment variable
options.rationale: Environment variables configure functions, not templates.

questions.explanation: Outputs with Export and Fn::ImportValue create cross-stack references.

questions.stem: A team wants to mark the exact commit that was released to production as version 2.3.0, so it can be found and redeployed later. What should the developer create?

options.text: A new branch for each file in the release
options.rationale: Branches track lines of work, not a single released commit.

options.text: A Git tag on that commit
options.rationale: Tags label specific commits, such as release versions.

options.text: A Lambda alias named 2.3.0
options.rationale: Aliases point to function versions, not source commits.

options.text: A pull request titled 2.3.0
options.rationale: Pull requests propose changes; they do not label a commit.

questions.explanation: Use tags for releases and branches for ongoing lines of development.

questions.stem: A team wants to run the Kiro agent inside its CI/CD pipeline, without an interactive sign-in, to check each deployment after it finishes. How can the pipeline run Kiro?

options.text: Install the Kiro IDE on the build server and open it for each run
options.rationale: The IDE needs an interactive user.

options.text: Add a Kiro steering file to the buildspec
options.rationale: Steering files guide the agent; they do not run it.

options.text: Use the Kiro CLI in headless mode with API key authentication
options.rationale: Headless mode lets the CLI run in automation without an interactive session.

options.text: Store a Kiro spec in Amazon ECR
options.rationale: ECR stores container images, not Kiro specs.

questions.explanation: The Kiro CLI supports headless use in pipelines for tasks such as post-deployment checks.
